L122: # Bacterial phenylalanine and phenylacetate catabolic pathway revealed

L137: cite82†PDF L138: ## Abstract
L139: Aromatic compounds constitute the second most abundant class of organic substrates and environmental pollutants, a substantial part of which (e.g., phenylalanine or styrene) is metabolized by bacteria via phenylacetate. Surprisingly, the bacterial catabolism of phenylalanine and phenylacetate remained an unsolved problem. Although a phenylacetate metabolic gene cluster had been identified, the underlying biochemistry remained largely unknown.
L140: Here we elucidate the catabolic pathway functioning in 16% of all bacteria whose genome has been sequenced, including Escherichia coli and Pseudomonas putida. This strategy is exceptional in several aspects. Intermediates are processed as CoA thioesters, and the aromatic ring of phenylacetyl-CoA becomes activated to a ring 1,2-epoxide by a distinct multicomponent oxygenase. The reactive nonaromatic epoxide is isomerized to a seven-member O-heterocyclic enol ether, an oxepin.
L141: This isomerization is followed by hydrolytic ring cleavage and β-oxidation steps, leading to acetyl-CoA and succinyl-CoA. This widespread paradigm differs significantly from the established chemistry of aerobic aromatic catabolism, thus widening our view of how organisms exploit such inert substrates. It provides insight into the natural remediation of man-made environmental contaminants such as styrene.
L142: Furthermore, this pathway occurs in various pathogens, where its reactive early intermediates may contribute to virulence.
L143: The biggest challenge for organisms using aromatic compounds as growth substrates is to overcome the stabilizing resonance energy of the aromatic ring system. This aromatic structure makes the substrates unreactive toward oxidation or reduction and thus requires elaborate degradation strategies. How microorganisms cope with this problem depends primarily on the availability of oxygen (cite83†1 ). Aerobic pathways use oxygen both for hydroxylation and for cleavage of the ring (cite84†2 , cite85†3 ).
L144: In contrast, under anaerobic conditions the common strategy consists of activation by CoA-thioester formation, shortening of the side chain, and energy-driven ring reduction, which also applies to phenylacetate catabolism (ref. cite86†4 and literature cited therein).
L145: The aerobic strategy is illustrated by the metabolism of phenylacetate and phenylacetyl-CoA, which are derived from a variety of substrates such as phenylalanine, lignin-related phenylpropane units, 2-phenylethylamine, phenylalkanoic acids with an even number of carbon atoms, or even environmental contaminants such as styrene and ethylbenzene (cite87†5 –cite88†7 ).
L146: Rarely, phenylalanine is hydroxylated to tyrosine, which can be converted into 4-hydroxyphenylpyruvate, followed by hydroxylation to homogentisate (2,5-dihydroxyphenylacetate) as the central intermediate. The aromatic ring of homogentisate then is split by a ring-cleaving homogentisate dioxygenase, and finally fumarate and acetoacetate are produced (cite89†8 ). In most cases, however, phenylalanine is converted into phenylacetate.
L147: A conventional aerobic route for phenylacetate, which also leads to homogentisate, occurs in fungi (cite90†9 ). In bacteria, generally, neither phenylalanine hydroxylation to tyrosine nor phenylacetate hydroxylation to homogentisate occurs, leaving unsolved the question of how most bacteria use phenylalanine or phenylacetate.
L148: Although first reports of aerobic phenylacetate-metabolizing bacteria appeared more than 50 y ago (cite91†10 ), the pathway itself remained enigmatic. The induction of a phenylacetate-CoA ligase in Pseudomonas putida under aerobic conditions was reported 2 decades ago (cite92†11 ). That report suggested an unconventional strategy for an oxygen-dependent metabolism using CoA-thioesters as intermediates (cite93†12 ).
L149: The ligase gene was found to be clustered together with 13 other phenylacetic acid (paa) genes in three transcriptional units, which were suspected to be involved in phenylacetate assimilation (cite94†13 ). Moreover, many of these genes were mandatory for growth on this substrate (cite95†14 ). A similar gene organization was reported in E. coli (cite96†15 ) (cite97†Fig.
L150: 1A ) and in several Pseudomonas species (cite94†13 , cite98†16 , cite99†17 ); the high sequence similarity allows the prediction of a similar structure and function of the homologous proteins in these organisms. It is the only known bacterial aerobic degradation pathway for phenylacetate and is the most common for phenylalanine.

L155: Many attempts to identify pathway intermediates other than phenylacetyl-CoA led only to rough outlines (cite95†14 , cite102†18 –cite103†20 ). We set out to elucidate the pathway for phenylacetate degradation by producing purified enzymes coded by the E. coli K12 and Pseudomonas sp. strain Y2 paa gene clusters.
L156: This widespread catabolic pathway differs fundamentally from known aromatic catabolic pathways and involves the use of CoA thioesters throughout, epoxide formation, isomerization of the epoxide to an oxepin, and hydrolytic ring cleavage.
L157: ## Results
L158: 
L159: The use of ^{13}C- and ^{14}C-labeled phenylacetate (cite97†Fig. 1B , compound I) was key to investigating this long-standing problem. These compounds were chemically transformed or enzymatically converted to phenylacetyl-CoA (cite97†Fig. 1B , compound II) using phenylacetate-CoA ligase (PaaK, the first enzyme of the pathway). Products were detected by UV and radioactivity detection and identified by ^{13}C-NMR spectroscopy, assisted by mass spectrometry.
L160: ### Epoxidation of the Aromatic Ring.
L161: Phenylacetyl-CoA is the substrate of a presumed multicomponent oxygenase, PaaABCDE. This oxygenase is a key enzyme of the pathway, proposed to be responsible for the introduction of oxygen into the aromatic ring of phenylacetyl-CoA (cite104†6 , cite95†14 , cite105†21 ). First we cloned the five genes encoding this enzyme. The genes for all subunits were expressed simultaneously with PaaA as a maltose-binding protein (mbp)-tagged protein. Purification carried out through amylose resin chromatography.
L162: Subunits PaaB, PaaC, and PaaE copurified with PaaA, whereas PaaD, a suspected subunit of this complex, eluted separately. The purified PaaABCE complex catalyzed a phenylacetyl-CoA–induced and strictly oxygen-dependent NADPH consumption in a spectrophotometric assay with ≈1 μmol min^{−1} mg^{−1} protein, implying phenylacetyl-CoA oxygenase/reductase activity. The product derived from phenylacetyl-CoA was highly unstable and was purified using reverse phase (RP)-HPLC (cite106†Fig. 2 A and B ).
L163: Mass spectrometry showed the incorporation of a single oxygen atom, suggesting the complex acts as a monooxygenase (cite107†Table 1 ). To identify PaaABC(D)E unambiguously as an oxygenase, we applied ^{18}O-labeling studies and showed the incorporation of a single ^{18}O atom from ^{18}O_{2} (cite107†Table 1 ). In contrast, no labeled oxygen was introduced to the ring when H_{2}^{18}O was used in the assay, clearly demonstrating the monooxygenase activity of PaaABC(D)E.
L164: ^{13}C-NMR analysis substantiated ring 1,2-epoxyphenylacetyl-CoA (cite97†Fig. 1B , compound III) as the product (cite108†Table 2 ). Further proof was provided by derivatization of the epoxide (cite107†Table 1 ). PaaABC(D)E thus functions as a ring 1,2-phenylacetyl-CoA epoxidase. Interestingly, the ability of PaaABC(D)E to oxygenate its substrate was largely lost within 5 min in an enzymatic assay. The multicomponent oxygenase thus appears to have been inactivated by its reactive epoxide product.
L165: To test a possible impact of PaaD on phenylacetyl-CoA oxygenation, we added purified mbp-tagged PaaD separately to the activity tests. The addition of the preparation did not affect the specific activity of PaaABCE significantly.

L232: ### C–C Bond Cleavage Through Isomerization.
L233: The paaG and paaZ knockout mutants of E. coli released 2-hydroxyphenylacetate when cultivated on phenylacetate (cite95†14 ), probably because of the decomposition of ring 1,2-epoxyphenylacetyl-CoA. Therefore these genes probably are involved in early steps of the pathway. We purified his-tagged PaaG and found that it catalyzed a reversible conversion of the epoxide to a new product (cite106†Fig. 2C ) that exhibited the same mass as the epoxide (cite107†Table 1 ).
L234: ^{13}C-NMR spectroscopy identified this isomer as an unusual unsaturated, oxygen-containing, seven-member heterocyclic enol ether, namely 2-oxepin-2(3H)-ylideneacetyl-CoA (oxepin-CoA) (cite97†Fig. 1B , compound IV and cite108†Table 2 ). PaaG therefore acted as a ring 1,2-epoxyphenylacetyl-CoA isomerase (oxepin-CoA–forming).
L235: ### Hydrolytic Ring Cleavage of the C–O Heterocycle.
L236: PaaZ is the most likely candidate for the ring-cleavage reaction. It is a fusion protein consisting of a C-terminal MaoC-like domain and an N-terminal aldehyde dehydrogenase domain. MaoC-like Hotdog-fold proteins act as R-specific hydratases (cite111†22 ). Addition of purified mbp-tagged PaaZ to enzymatically produced epoxide and oxepin (in the presence of PaaG) led to a complete NADP^{+}-dependent conversion of epoxide and oxepin into 3-oxo-5,6-dehydrosuberyl-CoA (cite97†Fig. 1B , compound V, and cite106†Fig.
L237: 2D ), as shown by mass spectrometry (cite107†Table 1 ) and ^{13}C-NMR spectroscopy (cite108†Table 2 ). PaaZ thus functioned as an oxepin-CoA hydrolase/ 3-oxo-5,6-dehydrosuberyl-CoA semialdehyde dehydrogenase catalyzing the two-step conversion of the oxepin-CoA via the open-chain aldehyde intermediate to 3-oxo-5,6-dehydrosuberyl-CoA (cite97†Fig. 1B ). This oxepin-CoA ring cleavage was affected by PaaZ with a specific activity of ≈20 μmol min^{−1} mg^{−1} protein.
L238: ### β-Oxidation of the Ring-Opened Intermediates.
L239: PaaJ, a β-ketothiolase, probably transforms the resulting β-keto C_{8} intermediate with CoA to the C_{6} intermediate dehydroadipyl-CoA (cite97†Fig. 1B , compound VI) and acetyl-CoA (cite97†Fig. 1B , compound VII) (cite95†14 ), besides catalyzing the last step of the pathway, in which 3-oxoadipyl-CoA similarly is cleaved to acetyl-CoA and succinyl-CoA. This last function has been shown previously (cite112†19 ).
L240: To test if the C_{8} compound also is a substrate for the β-ketothiolase, we added purified PaaJ to an enzymatic assay containing PaaABC(D)E, PaaG, and PaaZ. A complete conversion of 3-oxo-5,6-dehydrosuberyl-CoA into 2,3-dehydroadipyl-CoA and acetyl-CoA (cite97†Fig. 1B ) with accompanying CoA consumption was demonstrated by RP-HPLC (cite106†Fig. 2E ). The identity of the products was confirmed by mass spectrometry (cite107†Table 1 ) and ^{13}C-NMR spectroscopy (cite108†Table 2 ).
L241: PaaF is an enoyl-CoA hydratase. Purified PaaF, when added to the assay (cite106†Fig. 2E ), catalyzed the reversible conversion of enzymatically produced 2,3-dehydroadipyl-CoA into 3-hydroxyadipyl-CoA (cite97†Fig. 1B , compound VIII and cite106†Fig. 2F ), evidenced by mass spectrometry (cite107†Table 1 ). This analysis identified PaaF as a 2,3-dehydroadipyl-CoA hydratase (cite97†Fig. 1B ), in accordance with previous suggestions (cite95†14 ).
L242: PaaH is a member of the alcohol dehydrogenase family. To clarify the last steps of the aerobic phenylacetate pathway, we added purified mbp-tagged PaaH to enzymatically produced 3-hydroxyadipyl-CoA. We observed the formation of NADH, succinyl-CoA, and acetyl-CoA in the presence of CoA, NAD^{+}, and PaaJ (cite106†Fig. 2G ). PaaH therefore functioned as an NAD^{+}-dependent [probably (S)-3–specific] 3-hydroxyadipyl-CoA dehydrogenase forming 3-oxoadipyl-CoA (cite97†Fig. 1B , compound IX).
L243: PaaJ finally cleaved 3-oxoadipyl-CoA into the central metabolites succinyl-CoA (cite97†Fig. 1B , compound X) and acetyl-CoA (cite97†Fig. 1B , compound VII), completing the pathway.
L244: ## Discussion
L245: ### Unorthodox Aerobic Aromatic Degradation Strategy.
L246: This paradigm for aerobic aromatic catabolism differs significantly from established knowledge. The first enzyme of the pathway, phenylacetate-CoA ligase, converted phenylacetate into phenylacetyl-CoA (cite97†Fig. 1B ). All further intermediates likewise were processed as CoA-thioesters, a feature typical of anaerobic rather than aerobic aromatic metabolism.
L247: The identification of ring 1,2-epoxide as the second pathway intermediate is contrary to the formerly assumed dioxygenation of phenylacetyl-CoA to a dihydrodiol by a dioxygenase/reductase (cite95†14 ), a process that would have resembled conventional aerobic aromatic catabolism. Previous in silico studies designated PaaABC(D)E as the first member of a group of the family of bacterial di-iron multicomponent oxygenases acting on CoA-esters (cite105†21 ).
L248: This enzyme family consists exclusively of monooxygenases [e.g., methane monooxygenase (cite113†23 )], which also may form epoxides. The subunits PaaAC(D) probably act as the core oxygenase complex, because similar multicomponent oxygenases have been reported (cite114†24 ). PaaB probably acts as an effector protein, whereas PaaE likely functions as an iron-sulfur oxidoreductase transferring electrons from NADPH to the active center of the oxygenase complex (cite114†24 ).
L249: PaaD has been suggested to be part of the oxygenase complex (cite105†21 ), possibly acting as a stabilizing element (cite114†24 ). Alternatively, PaaD might not be a part of the catalytic complex, which may consist of two subunits instead of three, as known to occur in other members of the family (cite114†24 ). Sequence comparisons with the National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) database revealed the similarity of PaaD to proteins of the SUF operon.
L250: Proteins encoded by this operon are involved in the assembly of iron-sulfur clusters (cite115†25 ). The paaD-related gene is adjacent to the cysteine desulfurase gene sufS. A role in the assembly of iron-sulfur clusters is likely, although the actual function is unknown. PaaD therefore may take part in the formation of the predicted iron-sulfur cluster of the reductase subunit PaaE. Further studies are required to resolve this question.
